More often than not, literal interpretation of a statute or a provision of a statute results in absurdity.
Therefore, while interpreting statutory provisions, the Courts should keep in mind the objectives or
purpose for which statute has been enacted. Justice Frankfurter of U.S. Supreme Court in an article
titled as Some Reflections on the Reading of Statutes (47 Columbia Law Reports 527), observed that,
"legislation has an aim, it seeks to obviate some mischief, to supply an adequacy, to effect a change
of policy, to formulate a plan of Government. That aim, that policy is not drawn, like nitrogen, out of
the air; it is evidenced in the language of the statutes, as read in the light of other external
manifestations of purpose".

21. A reading of the proviso to sub-section (4) as well as the language employed in
sub-section (5) would indicate that they are intended to safeguard the interest of an
insurer who otherwise has no liability to pay any amount to the insured but for the
provisions contained in Chapter XI of the Act. This means, the insurer has to pay to
the third parties only on account of the fact that a policy of insurance has been issued
in respect of the vehicle, but the insurer is entitled to recover any such sum from the
insured if the insurer were not otherwise liable to pay such sum to the insured by
virtue of the conditions of the contract of insurance indicated by the policy.
22. To repeat, the effect of the above provisions is this:
when a valid insurance policy has been issued in respect of a vehicle as evidenced by
a certificate of insurance the burden is on the insurer to pay to the third parties,
whether or not there has been any breach or violation of the policy conditions. But
the amount so paid by the insurer to third parties can be allowed to be recovered
from the insured if as per the policy conditions the insurer had no liability to pay
such sum to the insured.

Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Kokilaben Chandravadan (1987 )2 SCC 654. Though the said
decision related to the corresponding provisions of the predecessor Act (Motor

Vehicles Act, 1939) the observations made in the judgment are quite germane now as
the corresponding provisions are materially the same as in the Act. Learned Judges
pointed out that the insistence of the legislature that a motor vehicle can be used in a
public place only if that vehicle is covered by a policy of insurance is not for the
purpose of promoting the business of the insurance company but to protect the
members of the community who become sufferers on account of accidents arising
from the use of motor vehicles. It is pointed out in the decision that such protection
would have remained only a paper protection if the compensation awarded by the
courts were not recoverable by the victims (or dependants of the victims) of the
accident.

args.question: Death caused by insured's truck whose driver had no valid licence — what precedents support National Insurance Co.'s defence, and which authorities cut against us?

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving a motor vehicle without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy. The insurer is not liable to indemnify the insured for such breach.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had NO driving licence at all — same as our case. The Tribunal held this was a fundamental breach proved by the insurer under Section 149(2).
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the strongest case in the corpus for establishing that 'no licence' is a fundamental breach. The Tribunal expressly held the insurer 'not liable to pay the compensation and absolved from its liability' to the insured, though it still ordered pay-and-recover for the third party.
supporting.quote: Hence, it is held that as rightly argued by the learned counsel for the respondent No.2 the respondent No.1 has breached the fundamental condition of the policy by allowing the driver who has no driving licence to drive the vehicle. ... riding/driving vehicle on public road without having driving license it is not only an offense punishable under section 3(1) r/w 181 of MV Act but also fundamental and statutory breach of insurance policy. Hence, the respondent No.2 is not liable to indemnify the respondent No.1 for the loss suffered by him though there was insurance on the date of accident.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: The insurer has a statutory liability to pay third-party compensation even where there is a breach (invalid licence), but is entitled to recover from the insured. The breach must be proved by the insurer.
supporting.fact_alignment: The court confirmed that proving the licence breach entitles the insurer to recovery rights. The corpus consistently holds that proving the breach is the insurer's burden, and once discharged, pay-and-recover follows.
supporting.why_it_matters: This judgment consolidates the entire line of Supreme Court authority (Skandia, Sohan Lal Passi, Kamla, Swaran Singh) and confirms that the insurer's statutory liability to third parties is coupled with a right of recovery. It provides the legal framework for our pay-and-recover argument.
supporting.quote: In view of the above discussion, there is no manner of doubt that the liability of the Insurance Company to satisfy the award in the first instance is statutory; it is bound to satisfy the same and will be entitled to recover the amount of compensation paid from the driver and the owner.

supporting.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
supporting.principle: Swaran Singh's principles apply only to third-party risks, not own-damage claims. A fake licence cannot be cured by subsequent renewal.
supporting.fact_alignment: While this case is about own-damage claims (not directly on point), it confirms the conceptual distinction between third-party and own-damage claims and reinforces that in third-party claims the insurer must pay and recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Useful to limit the scope of Swaran Singh — the Supreme Court itself clarified that Swaran Singh governs third-party claims. This helps us argue that the expansive 'purposive interpretation' from Swaran Singh does not extend beyond third-party contexts.
supporting.quote: The decision in Swaran Singh's case has no application to cases other than third party risks. ... In case of third party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised to recover the same from the insured.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where the driver holds only an LMV licence but drives a transport vehicle, there is a breach of policy conditions. The insurer must pay the third party and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had a licence but not for the class of vehicle driven — analogous to our case where the driver had no licence at all (a fortiori, our breach is more fundamental).
supporting.why_it_matters: Establishes that even a 'wrong class' licence is a breach. A fortiori, having no licence at all is a more serious breach. The court ordered pay-and-recover, which is the minimum relief we should expect.
supporting.quote: The 3rd Respondent had a licence, but not a valid one. As there was violation of conditions of policy, Tribunal was not right in fastening the statutory liability upon the Insurance Company. ... the only just and reasonable course would be to direct the Insurance Company to pay compensation to the 1st Respondent Claimant and recover it from the owner for his breach of the policy conditions.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
supporting.principle: Absence of a special endorsement required for driving hazardous goods vehicles constitutes a breach entitling the insurer to pay and recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: The insurer proved breach (missing endorsement) and the court granted pay-and-recover rights. Supports the principle that proving a licence defect leads to recovery rights.
supporting.why_it_matters: Demonstrates that courts routinely grant pay-and-recover when the insurer proves a licence-related breach. Useful as a procedural precedent for how recovery rights are framed.
supporting.quote: Once it was established that there was no such endorsement on the driving license of the driver of offending Tanker, then it was a clear cut case of violation of terms and conditions of the insurance policy which entitled the insurance company to recover the amount of compensation awarded by the Tribunal from the insured.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd., vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar W/O Late ...
supporting.principle: Where a driving licence had expired and was renewed after the accident, the driver did not hold a valid licence on the accident date. The insurer must pay and recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had no effective licence on the accident date (expired) — analogous to our 'no licence' scenario. The court ordered pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Reinforces that even a temporary lapse (expired licence) is a breach. Our case (no licence at all) is stronger. The court directed pay-and-recover, which is the minimum we should secure.
supporting.quote: Since it is the statutory right of the third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded either from the owner or the driver, as the vehicle in question is insured, the insurance company shall pay the amount and recover the same from driver or the insured.

supporting.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
supporting.principle: An insurer is bound to satisfy a third-party award even if breach is proved, and can recover from the insured. Complete absolution is possible only where fraud or collusion between victim and insured is established.
supporting.fact_alignment: This Full Bench decision confirms the general rule (pay-and-recover) but carves out a narrow exception for fraud/collusion cases. It also discusses the 'fundamental breach' concept.
supporting.why_it_matters: Provides the legal framework for when an insurer CAN be completely absolved — fraud/collusion between victim and insured. If our facts show any collusion or if the deceased contributed to the breach, this case supports complete exoneration.
supporting.quote: If fraud or collusion between the insured and the victim is established, in such an eventuality, the insurer is absolutely not liable to pay compensation though the case is covered under the policy.

adverse.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
adverse.principle: An insurer cannot avoid its statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties merely because the driver of a light motor vehicle did not have a specific endorsement on their licence to drive it as a commercial vehicle.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this Supreme Court judgment to argue that even if the driver lacked the proper licence/endorsement, the insurer remains liable to the third party. They will argue that the statutory liability under Section 149 is not defeated by licence defects.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: In S.Iyyapan, the driver DID hold a valid LMV licence — the dispute was only about the absence of a commercial endorsement. In our case, the driver had NO licence at all. The Supreme Court itself distinguished between 'holding a licence but lacking an endorsement' and 'having no licence'. Our case falls in the latter, more serious category. Additionally, S.Iyyapan was decided before the clarification in Laxmi Narain Dhut that Swaran Singh principles apply only to third-party claims.
adverse.quote: Merely because the driver did not get any endorsement in the driving licence to drive Mahindra Maxi Cab, which is a light motor vehicle, the High Court has committed grave error of law in holding that the insurer is not liable to pay compensation because the driver was not holding the licence to drive the commercial vehicle.

adverse.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
adverse.principle: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy a third-party award regardless of policy condition breaches such as an expired driving licence. Non-renewal of an otherwise valid licence does not constitute a fundamental breach absolving the insurer.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this to argue that even if the licence was invalid/expired, the insurer must still pay the third party. They will argue that the breach must be 'fundamental' and that merely lacking a valid licence is not enough to avoid liability.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case dealt with an expired licence that was subsequently renewed — the driver had historically held a valid licence. In our case, the driver had NO licence at all, which is a fundamentally different situation. The court in Srinivasamurthy itself noted that the driver 'was earlier having a valid driving licence' — the breach was merely a temporary lapse. No such mitigating factor exists here. Also, this is a 2001 Tribunal decision, which predates the Supreme Court's clarification in Swaran Singh and Laxmi Narain Dhut.
adverse.quote: The insurer is bound to satisfy the award passed against the third party and the conditions imposed in the policy would not bind the third party and the amount paid by the insurance company in view of the provisions of the Motor Vehicles Act can be recovered by the insurance company from the insured on proof of breach of condition of the policy.

adverse.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
adverse.principle: In third-party claims, even if the driver lacks an appropriate endorsement to drive a specific heavy vehicle class, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the third-party award and may recover from the insured.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this to argue that even if the driver was not licensed for a heavy goods vehicle (truck), the insurer must still pay the third party. This is factually close — our case involves a truck (heavy goods vehicle) driven without a valid licence.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: In Chennamma, the driver held an LMV licence with a transport vehicle endorsement — the dispute was whether that sufficed for a 'heavy goods vehicle'. The driver DID have some form of licence. In our case, the driver had NO licence whatsoever. The court in Chennamma expressly noted the driver 'had obtained licence for light motor vehicle' and had an endorsement for 'transport vehicle'. Our facts are materially worse from the insured's perspective.
adverse.quote: So far as the statutory liability of the insurer contemplated under the provisions of Motor Vehicles Act in the matter relating to the payment of compensation, the mere fact that there was violation of the terms and conditions subject to which the insurance policy has been issued, cannot have the effect of exonerating the insurer from the statutory liability cast upon him in this regard to pay the amount to the third party victim.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
adverse.principle: Where the driver holds only an LMV licence but drives a transport vehicle, there is a breach. The insurer must pay the third party and recover from the insured.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this to show that even where the court found a breach (wrong class of licence), the remedy was pay-and-recover, not exoneration. They will argue that the same result should follow here — the insurer pays, then recovers.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case actually supports our position that a licence defect is a breach. The only question is the remedy. We are not arguing for complete exoneration (unless fraud/collusion is shown); we are arguing for pay-and-recover, which this case grants. The claimant will use it to argue that pay-and-recover is the ceiling of what we can get, not the floor — but that is consistent with our primary position.
adverse.quote: The 3rd Respondent had a licence, but not a valid one. As there was violation of conditions of policy, ... the only just and reasonable course would be to direct the Insurance Company to pay compensation to the 1st Respondent Claimant and recover it from the owner for his breach of the policy conditions.

adverse.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
adverse.principle: Driving without a valid licence is a fundamental breach. The insurer is not liable to indemnify the insured, but must pay the third party and recover from the owner.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this to argue that even in the strongest 'no licence' case, the remedy was pay-and-recover, not complete exoneration. They will say: 'Even here, the third party was protected.'
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is actually one of our strongest supporting authorities — it establishes that 'no licence' is a fundamental breach. The claimant will use it only to argue the remedy point (pay-and-recover). We accept that pay-and-recover is the likely outcome; our strategy is to secure that and argue for complete exoneration only if the facts support fraud/collusion under the Yallavva framework.
adverse.quote: It is held that the respondent No.2 is not liable to pay the compensation and he is absolved from its liability. ... But, on the said ground, the petitioner is third party, cannot be made to suffer due to fault of owner when the vehicle is covered with insurance at relevant point of time.

adverse.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
adverse.principle: An insurer is bound to satisfy a third-party award even if breach is proved, and can recover from the insured. Complete absolution requires fraud or collusion.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this Full Bench decision for the proposition that the general rule is pay-and-recover, and that complete exoneration is reserved for exceptional cases of fraud/collusion. They will argue that our case does not meet that high threshold.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case actually helps us by providing the legal framework. It confirms that if we prove the breach, we get pay-and-recover. It also leaves open the possibility of complete exoneration in fraud/collusion cases — if our facts support it. The claimant's reliance on this case only reinforces our primary position.
adverse.quote: Pursuant to the mandate of Section 149(1) and (4) of the Motor Vehicles Act 1988, an insurer is bound to satisfy a third-party judgment or award as a judgment debtor and recover the amount from the insured even if a breach of policy conditions under Section 149(2) is successfully proved, unless fraud or collusion between the victim and the insured is established.

priority_arguments: 1. Fundamental breach: The driver had NO driving licence at all — this is the most serious category of licence defect. Cite doc_024 (Sunil Shreesail Killiket) which expressly holds that driving without a licence is a 'fundamental and statutory breach' and that the insurer is 'absolved from its liability' to the insured.

2. Pay-and-recover: In the alternative, even if the Tribunal holds the insurer liable to the third party, seek a clear pay-and-recover order against the owner. The entire corpus (doc_033 Satto, doc_035 Vijayakumar, doc_001 Neelam Devi, doc_003 Parvathi Hebbar, doc_027 Chennamma) supports this as the minimum relief.

3. Burden of proof: The insurer must prove the breach. Ensure the charge sheet, RTO verification, and any admission by the owner/driver are on record. Doc_024 shows that non-production of the driving licence by the owner supports an adverse inference.

4. Complete exoneration (if facts permit): Under doc_025 (Yallavva), if there is any evidence of fraud or collusion between the deceased and the insured (e.g., the deceased knew the driver had no licence, or the accident was staged), argue for complete absolution of the insurer.

5. Quantum challenge: Independently, scrutinise the quantum claimed. Use doc_007 (Harpreet Singh) to argue that non-dependent legal representatives cannot claim loss of dependency. Use the compute_quantum tool to verify the arithmetic.
strategy.compensation_range: Cannot estimate without knowing the deceased's income, age, and number of dependents. The corpus shows awards ranging from approximately Rs. 2.45 lakhs (doc_003, 2017, modest income) to Rs. 17.53 lakhs (doc_007, 2014, government employee). Use compute_quantum with actual figures.
strategy.compensation_reasoning: The quantum will depend on the deceased's income, age, and number of dependents under the Sarla Verma / Pranay Sethi framework. The licence-defect issue does not affect quantum — it affects who pays. Our primary goal is to ensure the liability is ultimately borne by the owner, not the insurer.
risks: 1. The Tribunal may order pay-and-recover without expressly recording the breach as 'fundamental', which could weaken our recovery rights. Ensure the judgment explicitly records the finding of breach under Section 149(2)(a)(ii).
2. If the owner is untraceable or insolvent, a pay-and-recover order may be practically unenforceable. Consider seeking a direction for the owner to furnish security.

3. The claimant may argue that the owner made bona fide inquiries about the licence (doc_034 Srinivasamurthy). Anticipate this and ensure evidence that no reasonable inquiry was made — the driver had no licence at all.
4. S.Iyyapan (doc_032) is a Supreme Court judgment that the claimant will heavily rely on. Distinguish it on facts: in Iyyapan, the driver held a valid LMV licence; here, the driver had no licence.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: Claims Tribunal under Section 166 MV Act. Primary relief: exoneration of the insurer on the ground that the driver had no licence, constituting a fundamental breach. Alternative relief: pay-and-recover order against the owner with liberty to execute the award against the owner's assets. Ensure the award explicitly records: (a) the finding of breach under Section 149(2)(a)(ii), (b) the insurer's right to recover the entire sum paid, with interest, from the owner, and (c) the mode of recovery (execution under Section 174 or independent proceedings).

caveats: 1. The corpus does not contain any judgment where an insurer was completely exonerated from paying third-party compensation solely on the ground that the driver had no licence. The consistent position across all relevant judgments is pay-and-recover. Complete exoneration under doc_025 (Yallavva) requires fraud or collusion between the victim and the insured.

2. Several judgments in the corpus deal with gratuitous passengers in goods vehicles (doc_014 Shivlal, doc_029 Mahesh Kanubhai) — these are not relevant to our case unless the deceased was a gratuitous passenger rather than a third-party road user.

3. Doc_009 (Kamal vs Mursleem) deals with contributory negligence of an injured rider who had no licence — this is distinguishable as it involves an injured claimant who himself was driving without a licence, not a third-party death claim.

4. Doc_005 (L And T Insurance vs Bindudevi) and doc_006 (Meena) deal with issues under the Workmen's Compensation Act and contributory negligence respectively — not relevant to the licence-defence issue.

payload.ratio: A trailer attached to a tractor is considered part of the tractor and does not require separate insurance under the Motor Vehicles Act; however, if the tractor is used for non-agricultural purposes in violation of the insurance policy, the insurer is not liable to pay compensation.

args.question: Death caused by insured's truck whose driver had no valid licence — what precedents support National Insurance Co.'s defence, and which authorities cut against us?

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving a motor vehicle without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy. The insurer is not liable to indemnify the insured for such breach.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had NO driving licence at all — same as our case. The Tribunal held this was a fundamental breach proved by the insurer under Section 149(2).
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the strongest case in the corpus for establishing that 'no licence' is a fundamental breach. The Tribunal expressly held the insurer 'not liable to pay the compensation and absolved from its liability' to the insured, though it still ordered pay-and-recover for the third party.
supporting.quote: Hence, it is held that as rightly argued by the learned counsel for the respondent No.2 the respondent No.1 has breached the fundamental condition of the policy by allowing the driver who has no driving licence to drive the vehicle. ... riding/driving vehicle on public road without having driving license it is not only an offense punishable under section 3(1) r/w 181 of MV Act but also fundamental and statutory breach of insurance policy. Hence, the respondent No.2 is not liable to indemnify the respondent No.1 for the loss suffered by him though there was insurance on the date of accident.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: The insurer has a statutory liability to pay third-party compensation even where there is a breach (invalid licence), but is entitled to recover from the insured. The breach must be proved by the insurer.
supporting.fact_alignment: The court confirmed that proving the licence breach entitles the insurer to recovery rights. The corpus consistently holds that proving the breach is the insurer's burden, and once discharged, pay-and-recover follows.
supporting.why_it_matters: This judgment consolidates the entire line of Supreme Court authority (Skandia, Sohan Lal Passi, Kamla, Swaran Singh) and confirms that the insurer's statutory liability to third parties is coupled with a right of recovery. It provides the legal framework for our pay-and-recover argument.
supporting.quote: In view of the above discussion, there is no manner of doubt that the liability of the Insurance Company to satisfy the award in the first instance is statutory; it is bound to satisfy the same and will be entitled to recover the amount of compensation paid from the driver and the owner.

supporting.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
supporting.principle: Swaran Singh's principles apply only to third-party risks, not own-damage claims. A fake licence cannot be cured by subsequent renewal.
supporting.fact_alignment: While this case is about own-damage claims (not directly on point), it confirms the conceptual distinction between third-party and own-damage claims and reinforces that in third-party claims the insurer must pay and recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Useful to limit the scope of Swaran Singh — the Supreme Court itself clarified that Swaran Singh governs third-party claims. This helps us argue that the expansive 'purposive interpretation' from Swaran Singh does not extend beyond third-party contexts.
supporting.quote: The decision in Swaran Singh's case has no application to cases other than third party risks. ... In case of third party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised to recover the same from the insured.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where the driver holds only an LMV licence but drives a transport vehicle, there is a breach of policy conditions. The insurer must pay the third party and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had a licence but not for the class of vehicle driven — analogous to our case where the driver had no licence at all (a fortiori, our breach is more fundamental).
supporting.why_it_matters: Establishes that even a 'wrong class' licence is a breach. A fortiori, having no licence at all is a more serious breach. The court ordered pay-and-recover, which is the minimum relief we should expect.
supporting.quote: The 3rd Respondent had a licence, but not a valid one. As there was violation of conditions of policy, Tribunal was not right in fastening the statutory liability upon the Insurance Company. ... the only just and reasonable course would be to direct the Insurance Company to pay compensation to the 1st Respondent Claimant and recover it from the owner for his breach of the policy conditions.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
supporting.principle: Absence of a special endorsement required for driving hazardous goods vehicles constitutes a breach entitling the insurer to pay and recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: The insurer proved breach (missing endorsement) and the court granted pay-and-recover rights. Supports the principle that proving a licence defect leads to recovery rights.
supporting.why_it_matters: Demonstrates that courts routinely grant pay-and-recover when the insurer proves a licence-related breach. Useful as a procedural precedent for how recovery rights are framed.
supporting.quote: Once it was established that there was no such endorsement on the driving license of the driver of offending Tanker, then it was a clear cut case of violation of terms and conditions of the insurance policy which entitled the insurance company to recover the amount of compensation awarded by the Tribunal from the insured.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd., vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar W/O Late ...
supporting.principle: Where a driving licence had expired and was renewed after the accident, the driver did not hold a valid licence on the accident date. The insurer must pay and recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had no effective licence on the accident date (expired) — analogous to our 'no licence' scenario. The court ordered pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Reinforces that even a temporary lapse (expired licence) is a breach. Our case (no licence at all) is stronger. The court directed pay-and-recover, which is the minimum we should secure.
supporting.quote: Since it is the statutory right of the third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded either from the owner or the driver, as the vehicle in question is insured, the insurance company shall pay the amount and recover the same from driver or the insured.

supporting.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
supporting.principle: An insurer is bound to satisfy a third-party award even if breach is proved, and can recover from the insured. Complete absolution is possible only where fraud or collusion between victim and insured is established.
supporting.fact_alignment: This Full Bench decision confirms the general rule (pay-and-recover) but carves out a narrow exception for fraud/collusion cases. It also discusses the 'fundamental breach' concept.
supporting.why_it_matters: Provides the legal framework for when an insurer CAN be completely absolved — fraud/collusion between victim and insured. If our facts show any collusion or if the deceased contributed to the breach, this case supports complete exoneration.
supporting.quote: If fraud or collusion between the insured and the victim is established, in such an eventuality, the insurer is absolutely not liable to pay compensation though the case is covered under the policy.

supporting.title: National Insurance Co.Ltd. vs Harpreet Singh And Ors.
supporting.principle: A legal representative who was not dependent upon the deceased at the time of death is not entitled to compensation under the head 'loss of dependency'.
supporting.fact_alignment: If any of the claimants are not financially dependent on the deceased (e.g., adult employed children), this case supports reducing the quantum by excluding them from dependency calculation.
supporting.why_it_matters: Useful for quantum challenge. If the deceased's family includes non-dependent members, we can argue for a higher deduction (1/2 instead of 1/3) and exclusion of those claimants from loss of dependency.
supporting.quote: A legal representative of a victim of a motor accident, who was not dependent upon the deceased, though can lay a claim for compensation, he is not entitled to compensation under the head 'loss of dependency'.

adverse.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
adverse.principle: An insurer cannot avoid its statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties merely because the driver of a light motor vehicle did not have a specific endorsement on their licence to drive it as a commercial vehicle.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this Supreme Court judgment to argue that even if the driver lacked the proper licence/endorsement, the insurer remains liable to the third party. They will argue that the statutory liability under Section 149 is not defeated by licence defects.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: In S.Iyyapan, the driver DID hold a valid LMV licence — the dispute was only about the absence of a commercial endorsement. The Supreme Court itself distinguished between 'holding a licence but lacking an endorsement' and 'having no licence'. Our case falls in the latter, more serious category. Additionally, S.Iyyapan was decided before the clarification in Laxmi Narain Dhut that Swaran Singh principles apply only to third-party claims.
adverse.quote: Merely because the driver did not get any endorsement in the driving licence to drive Mahindra Maxi Cab, which is a light motor vehicle, the High Court has committed grave error of law in holding that the insurer is not liable to pay compensation because the driver was not holding the licence to drive the commercial vehicle.

adverse.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
adverse.principle: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy a third-party award regardless of policy condition breaches such as an expired driving licence. Non-renewal of an otherwise valid licence does not constitute a fundamental breach absolving the insurer.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this to argue that even if the licence was invalid/expired, the insurer must still pay the third party. They will argue that the breach must be 'fundamental' and that merely lacking a valid licence is not enough to avoid liability.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case dealt with an expired licence that was subsequently renewed — the driver had historically held a valid licence. In our case, the driver had NO licence at all, which is a fundamentally different situation. The court in Srinivasamurthy itself noted that the driver 'was earlier having a valid driving licence' — the breach was merely a temporary lapse. No such mitigating factor exists here. Also, this is a 2001 Tribunal decision, which predates the Supreme Court's clarification in Swaran Singh and Laxmi Narain Dhut.
adverse.quote: The insurer is bound to satisfy the award passed against the third party and the conditions imposed in the policy would not bind the third party and the amount paid by the insurance company in view of the provisions of the Motor Vehicles Act can be recovered by the insurance company from the insured on proof of breach of condition of the policy.

adverse.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
adverse.principle: In third-party claims, even if the driver lacks an appropriate endorsement to drive a specific heavy vehicle class, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the third-party award and may recover from the insured.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this to argue that even if the driver was not licensed for a heavy goods vehicle (truck), the insurer must still pay the third party. This is factually close — our case involves a truck (heavy goods vehicle) driven without a valid licence.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: In Chennamma, the driver held an LMV licence with a transport vehicle endorsement — the dispute was whether that sufficed for a 'heavy goods vehicle'. The driver DID have some form of licence. In our case, the driver had NO licence whatsoever. The court in Chennamma expressly noted the driver 'had obtained licence for light motor vehicle' and had an endorsement for 'transport vehicle'. Our facts are materially worse from the insured's perspective.
adverse.quote: So far as the statutory liability of the insurer contemplated under the provisions of Motor Vehicles Act in the matter relating to the payment of compensation, the mere fact that there was violation of the terms and conditions subject to which the insurance policy has been issued, cannot have the effect of exonerating the insurer from the statutory liability cast upon him in this regard to pay the amount to the third party victim.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
adverse.principle: Where the driver holds only an LMV licence but drives a transport vehicle, there is a breach. The insurer must pay the third party and recover from the insured.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this to show that even where the court found a breach (wrong class of licence), the remedy was pay-and-recover, not exoneration. They will argue that the same result should follow here — the insurer pays, then recovers.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case actually supports our position that a licence defect is a breach. The only question is the remedy. We are not arguing for complete exoneration (unless fraud/collusion is shown); we are arguing for pay-and-recover, which this case grants. The claimant will use it to argue that pay-and-recover is the ceiling of what we can get, not the floor — but that is consistent with our primary position.
adverse.quote: The 3rd Respondent had a licence, but not a valid one. As there was violation of conditions of policy, ... the only just and reasonable course would be to direct the Insurance Company to pay compensation to the 1st Respondent Claimant and recover it from the owner for his breach of the policy conditions.

adverse.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
adverse.principle: Driving without a valid licence is a fundamental breach. The insurer is not liable to indemnify the insured, but must pay the third party and recover from the owner.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this to argue that even in the strongest 'no licence' case, the remedy was pay-and-recover, not complete exoneration. They will say: 'Even here, the third party was protected.'
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is actually one of our strongest supporting authorities — it establishes that 'no licence' is a fundamental breach. The claimant will use it only to argue the remedy point (pay-and-recover). We accept that pay-and-recover is the likely outcome; our strategy is to secure that and argue for complete exoneration only if the facts support fraud/collusion under the Yallavva framework.
adverse.quote: It is held that the respondent No.2 is not liable to pay the compensation and he is absolved from its liability. ... But, on the said ground, the petitioner is third party, cannot be made to suffer due to fault of owner when the vehicle is covered with insurance at relevant point of time.

adverse.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
adverse.principle: An insurer is bound to satisfy a third-party award even if breach is proved, and can recover from the insured. Complete absolution requires fraud or collusion.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this Full Bench decision for the proposition that the general rule is pay-and-recover, and that complete exoneration is reserved for exceptional cases of fraud/collusion. They will argue that our case does not meet that high threshold.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case actually helps us by providing the legal framework. It confirms that if we prove the breach, we get pay-and-recover. It also leaves open the possibility of complete exoneration in fraud/collusion cases — if our facts support it. The claimant's reliance on this case only reinforces our primary position.
adverse.quote: Pursuant to the mandate of Section 149(1) and (4) of the Motor Vehicles Act 1988, an insurer is bound to satisfy a third-party judgment or award as a judgment debtor and recover the amount from the insured even if a breach of policy conditions under Section 149(2) is successfully proved, unless fraud or collusion between the victim and the insured is established.

priority_arguments: 1. Fundamental breach: The driver had NO driving licence at all — this is the most serious category of licence defect. Cite doc_024 (Sunil Shreesail Killiket) which expressly holds that driving without a licence is a 'fundamental and statutory breach' and that the insurer is 'absolved from its liability' to the insured.

2. Pay-and-recover: In the alternative, even if the Tribunal holds the insurer liable to the third party, seek a clear pay-and-recover order against the owner. The entire corpus (doc_033 Satto, doc_035 Vijayakumar, doc_001 Neelam Devi, doc_003 Parvathi Hebbar, doc_027 Chennamma) supports this as the minimum relief.

3. Burden of proof: The insurer must prove the breach. Ensure the charge sheet, RTO verification, and any admission by the owner/driver are on record. Doc_024 shows that non-production of the driving licence by the owner supports an adverse inference.

4. Complete exoneration (if facts permit): Under doc_025 (Yallavva), if there is any evidence of fraud or collusion between the deceased and the insured (e.g., the deceased knew the driver had no licence, or the accident was staged), argue for complete absolution of the insurer.

5. Quantum challenge: Independently, scrutinise the quantum claimed. Use doc_007 (Harpreet Singh) to argue that non-dependent legal representatives cannot claim loss of dependency. Use the compute_quantum tool to verify the arithmetic.
strategy.compensation_range: Cannot estimate without knowing the deceased's income, age, and number of dependents. The corpus shows awards ranging from approximately Rs. 2.45 lakhs (doc_003, 2017, modest income) to Rs. 17.53 lakhs (doc_007, 2014, government employee). Use compute_quantum with actual figures.
strategy.compensation_reasoning: The quantum will depend on the deceased's income, age, and number of dependents under the Sarla Verma / Pranay Sethi framework. The licence-defect issue does not affect quantum — it affects who pays. Our primary goal is to ensure the liability is ultimately borne by the owner, not the insurer.
risks: 1. The Tribunal may order pay-and-recover without expressly recording the breach as 'fundamental', which could weaken our recovery rights. Ensure the judgment explicitly records the finding of breach under Section 149(2)(a)(ii).
2. If the owner is untraceable or insolvent, a pay-and-recover order may be practically unenforceable. Consider seeking a direction for the owner to furnish security.

3. The claimant may argue that the owner made bona fide inquiries about the licence (doc_034 Srinivasamurthy). Anticipate this and ensure evidence that no reasonable inquiry was made — the driver had no licence at all.
4. S.Iyyapan (doc_032) is a Supreme Court judgment that the claimant will heavily rely on. Distinguish it on facts: in Iyyapan, the driver held a valid LMV licence; here, the driver had no licence.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: Claims Tribunal under Section 166 MV Act. Primary relief: exoneration of the insurer on the ground that the driver had no licence, constituting a fundamental breach. Alternative relief: pay-and-recover order against the owner with liberty to execute the award against the owner's assets. Ensure the award explicitly records: (a) the finding of breach under Section 149(2)(a)(ii), (b) the insurer's right to recover the entire sum paid, with interest, from the owner, and (c) the mode of recovery (execution under Section 174 or independent proceedings).

caveats: doc_002 (Liyakat Ali): About tractor used for non-agricultural purposes violating policy — insurer absolved. Not about licence defect. Irrelevant to our case.

doc_009 (Kamal vs Mursleem): The injured claimant himself was driving without a licence — contributory negligence applied. Our case involves a third-party death, not the claimant driving. Distinguishable.
doc_016 (State of HP): Criminal revision about bus driver. Holds that absence of licence does not prove rashness/negligence in criminal law. Not about civil compensation under MV Act. Irrelevant.
doc_017 (Sanjay vs State of Haryana): Criminal revision about rash driving conviction. Not about civil compensation or insurer liability for licence breach. Irrelevant.
doc_026 (Ellappa): About passengers in goods vehicle — insurer not statutorily liable for gratuitous passengers. Not about licence defect. Irrelevant.
doc_028 (Sukumarbai): About passengers in private vehicle for hire — insurer completely exonerated. Not about licence defect. Irrelevant.
doc_030 (Dadapeera): About person on tractor mud-guard — insurer not liable. Not about licence defect. Irrelevant.
doc_038 (Crown Consultants): Consumer dispute about claim repudiation — not a motor accident compensation case. Irrelevant.
doc_051 (Yashpal Chaudhrani): Criminal quashing petition — not a motor accident case. Irrelevant.
doc_054 (Chinnasamy): Civil suit for specific performance — not a motor accident case. Irrelevant.
doc_005 (L And T Insurance vs Bindudevi): About bar under Section 167 MV Act and Workmen's Compensation — not about licence defect. Irrelevant.
doc_006 (Meena): About contributory negligence and evidence — not about licence defect. Irrelevant.
doc_014 (Shivlal): About gratuitous passenger in goods vehicle — insurer not liable. Not about licence defect. Irrelevant.
